chapters.title: Strategy and Strategic Management: Concept and Process
chapters.scope: What strategy is, what strategic management adds, the four-step process, and how strategic decisions actually get made.

blocks.title: What strategy is
blocks.html:
A kirana owner has saved ₹10 lakh. She could add a cold store, open a second shop or start home delivery, but not all three. And a supermarket may open down the road next year.

In plain wordsStrategy is a plan for using limited resources to reach your aims when you cannot be sure what others will do.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a strategy is an organisation's plan for using its limited resources to reach its objectives in an uncertain world.

A strategy integrates the organisation's activities and commits resources for the long term. It takes account of how customers, competitors and employees are likely to behave. Writers have defined it in several ways.

WriterStrategy is…
Alfred Chandler, Strategy and Structure (1962)the determination of the basic long-term goals and objectives of an enterprise, and the adoption of courses of action and the allocation of resources necessary for carrying out these goals
Thompson and Stricklandthe means (actions) by which the ends (objectives) are achieved
Michael Porter, Competitive Strategy (1980)a combination of the ends for which the firm is striving and the means by which it is seeking to get there
Michael Porter, “What Is Strategy?” (1996)being different: deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value

Features. Strategy is needed because the future cannot be foreseen. It deals with long-term developments, such as new products, methods and markets, rather than routine operations. It anticipates the behaviour of customers, competitors and employees. And it is a roadmap that sets direction, building on the organisation's strengths and blunting rivals' advantages.

Mintzberg's five Ps. Henry Mintzberg (1987) noted that the word is used in five senses. The kirana store shows each one.

Strategy as…MeaningAt the kirana store
PlanA course of action decided in advanceA decision to open a second shop next year
PloyA manoeuvre to outwit a rivalStarting free home delivery just before the supermarket opens
PatternConsistency in a stream of actions, intended or notOver ten years she has always stocked local brands first, without ever deciding to
PositionA place in the marketThe shop the street trusts for monthly credit
PerspectiveThe organisation's way of seeing the worldHer belief that the shop wins by knowing every customer by name

Don't confuse strategy with operational effectiveness. In Porter's 1996 argument, doing the same activities better than rivals is operational effectiveness. It matters, but rivals can copy it. Strategy means doing different activities, or similar ones in different ways.

Where it breaks. Strategy as a plan assumes managers can see far enough ahead to plan. Often they cannot, and the strategy is visible only afterwards, as a pattern. That is why Mintzberg's other Ps matter.

For exams. Match each definition to its writer and year, and learn the five Ps.

Strategy bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to be.

blocks.title: What strategic management is
blocks.html:
A chain of six bakeries writes a careful five-year plan. A year later, no budget, shop or job has changed. The strategy was written down, but nobody managed it.

In plain wordsStrategic management is the whole job of choosing a strategy, putting it into action and checking whether it works.

Exam definitionStrategic management is “the art and science of formulating, implementing and evaluating cross-functional decisions that enable an organization to achieve its objectives” (Fred R. David).

It is the stream of decisions and actions through which an organisation develops and carries out its strategies. It is found in businesses, cooperatives, government bodies and non-profits alike. It integrates management, marketing, finance and accounting, production and operations, research and development, and information systems.

WriterStrategic management…
Brackeranalyses a firm's internal and external environments to make the best use of its resources in relation to its objectives
Jemisonis the process by which general managers of complex organisations develop and use a strategy to co-align the organisation's competence with the opportunities and constraints in its environment
Van Cauwenbergh and Cooldeals with the formulation (policy) and implementation (organisation) of calculated behaviour in new situations, and is the basis for later administration when the circumstances repeat
Schendel and Coolis the entrepreneur's work of starting organisations and, since corporations live on, of renewing them

Against long-range planning. In David's contrast, strategic management seeks to exploit and create new and different opportunities for tomorrow. Long-range planning tries to optimise for tomorrow the trends of today. The bakeries show the difference.

ApproachThe bakeries' question
Long-range planningSales have grown each year, so where do we open two more shops of the same kind?
Strategic managementOffice workers now order breakfast online. Should we open a delivery-only kitchen instead?

Objectives. Strategic management aims:

  • to exploit and create new opportunities;
  • to give managers a framework linking actions, context and performance;
  • to win a competitive position and sustain it, by acquiring and deploying the right resources and monitoring the environment;
  • to respond to key stakeholders;
  • to find, attract and keep customers.

The result is a strategic plan, the company's game plan. It is a set of hard choices among good alternatives that commits the firm to particular markets, policies and operations.

Don't confuse strategic management with strategic planning. The two are often used as synonyms, more in business than in academic writing. In the narrower sense, strategic planning means formulation only. Strategic management covers formulation, implementation and evaluation.

Where it breaks. Strategic management can shrink into a yearly paperwork ritual, with plans filed and forgotten. Too much analysis can also delay action until the opportunity has passed.

For exams. Learn David's definition, his contrast with long-range planning, and the narrow meaning of strategic planning.

blocks.title: The strategic management process
blocks.html:
Picture a tiffin service in Pune that loses half its office customers when offices empty. Its owner must notice the change, choose a response, carry it out and check that it worked, and then do it all again.

In plain wordsThe strategic management process is the repeating cycle of studying the situation, choosing a strategy, carrying it out and checking the results.

Exam definitionA standard textbook account: the strategic management process consists of four steps, environmental scanning, strategy formulation, strategy implementation and strategy evaluation.

The steps are carried out in order when a strategy is first made. They are revisited whenever the situation demands.

StepWhat happensAt the tiffin service
1 Environmental scanningCollecting, scrutinising and passing on information about the internal and external factors that affect the organisation: its strengths and weaknesses, opportunities and threatsOffices are half empty, but more people now work from home nearby
2 Strategy formulationDeciding the best course of action to reach the objectives: corporate, business and functional strategiesDeliver to homes in three nearby areas on a monthly subscription
3 Strategy implementationPutting the chosen strategy into action: designing the structure, allocating resources, setting up decision processes and managing peopleRe-plan delivery routes, buy two scooters, take orders on a messaging app
4 Strategy evaluationReviewing the internal and external factors on which the strategy rests, measuring performance, and taking corrective actionCount subscribers and margin each month; drop the area that does not pay

The aim is strategic alignment: making the organisation's resources, structure and capabilities support its long-term objectives. Scooters, routes and staff all have to serve the new home-delivery strategy.

Don't confuse formulation with implementation. Formulation chooses what to do; implementation makes it happen through structure, resources and people. Some textbooks, such as Fred David's, describe three stages, formulation, implementation and evaluation, and treat scanning as part of formulation.

Where it breaks. Real organisations rarely move through the steps one at a time. Implementation often reveals facts that change the formulation, and scanning never stops.

For exams. Know the order of the four steps and place an activity in its step: allocating resources is implementation, measuring performance is evaluation.

Scan, formulate, implement, evaluate, and begin again.

blocks.title: Modes of strategic decision-making
blocks.html:
A founder-led start-up, a state university and a large conglomerate all make strategy, but in very different ways. Knowing which way your organisation works tells you how to get a decision made in it.

In plain wordsA mode of strategic decision-making is the usual way strategy actually gets made in an organisation.

Exam definitionA standard textbook account: Henry Mintzberg (1973) described three modes of strategy-making, entrepreneurial, adaptive and planning.

ModeHow strategy is madeTypical of
EntrepreneurialOne powerful individual, usually the founder, makes bold, risky decisions guided by a personal vision. The search for opportunities comes first; problems are secondary.Young, founder-led firms
AdaptiveReactive, step-by-step solutions to existing problems, with much bargaining over priorities. Strategy is fragmented and moves the organisation forward in small steps; Charles Lindblom (1959) called this “muddling through”.Universities, large hospitals, many government agencies
PlanningAnalysts gather information systematically, generate alternatives and choose rationally among them, both seeking new opportunities and solving existing problems.Large corporations

Logical incrementalism, a fourth mode, was added by James Brian Quinn (Strategies for Change, 1980). Top management first sets a reasonably clear mission and objectives. Strategy then emerges through probing the future, experimenting and learning from a series of partial commitments, rather than one grand plan. It suits a fast-changing environment, a need to build consensus, and a need to develop resources before committing the whole company.

Deliberate and emergent strategy (Mintzberg and James Waters, 1985). A deliberate strategy is realised as intended. An emergent strategy is a pattern of action that forms over time without, or despite, intentions. The strategy an organisation actually follows, its realised strategy, is usually a mix of the two. Some intended strategy is never realised.

Don't confuse logical incrementalism with the adaptive mode. Both move in small steps. In logical incrementalism, top management sets a clear mission first and the steps are deliberate experiments toward it. In the adaptive mode there is no clear goal; steps come from bargaining over today's problems. Nor is emergent strategy the same as having no strategy: it is still a consistent pattern, just not one planned in advance.

Where it breaks. The modes are ideal types. Most organisations mix them, and a firm can shift mode as it grows: a founder's start-up may adopt formal planning once it is large.

For exams. Match each mode to its author and year, its features and the organisations it typifies. Know the three kinds of strategy in Mintzberg and Waters: deliberate, emergent and realised.

Go deeper for practitioners

The limits of planning. In The Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning (1994), Mintzberg argued that formal planning cannot create strategy on its own. Analysis breaks a problem into parts, while strategy needs synthesis. Planning helps most in turning a strategy already chosen into budgets and programmes, and in spotting patterns as they emerge.

A decision. A Pune auto-parts maker built its business on carmakers. Over three years, one-off orders from a tractor maker have grown, as an illustration, to ₹30 crore of its ₹120 crore sales, a quarter. Nobody planned this; it is an emergent strategy. Should the board make it deliberate, with a tractor-parts team and budget, or treat it as a distraction from cars? Either way, the board should decide now, not drift.

Links. Strategic intent (the next chapter) is the clear direction that logical incrementalism assumes. Strategy implementation and evaluation shows how a chosen strategy is carried through.

Strategy can be planned, improvised, bargained over or learned along the way.

text: The Kuṟaḷ asks that before any action one weigh what will be lost, what will be gained, and what yield will follow. That is the core of a strategy: choosing a course of action and committing resources only after counting its costs and returns.

text: Before acting, the Kuṟaḷ says, look at how the work will end, what obstacles stand in the way, and what gain it will bring. The process asks the same of a strategy: scanning for obstacles, formulating toward an end, and evaluating whether the gain arrived. The couplet is about a single undertaking, not a continuing cycle.

chapters.title: Strategic Intent: Vision, Mission, Goals and Objectives
chapters.scope: The hierarchy of purpose that tells everyone where the organisation is heading, why it exists and what it must achieve.

blocks.title: Strategic intent and the hierarchy of purpose
blocks.html:
Tell a team only "be the best" and nobody knows what to do on Monday. Tell it only "raise sales 8%" and nobody knows why it matters. Strategic intent, and the ladder of statements below it, joins the two.

In plain wordsStrategic intent is a big, long-term ambition to win a position that lies beyond what the organisation can do today.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: strategic intent is an organisation's long-term aspiration to win a desired position, with a strong competitive focus. It stretches the organisation's resources and core competencies toward goals that may at first seem out of reach.

Gary Hamel and C. K. Prahalad made the term famous in a 1989 Harvard Business Review article. By setting a goal that looks out of reach, strategic intent clarifies priorities, focuses effort and motivates people.

Example. Picture an auto-parts maker in Pune that today supplies brake parts to two Indian carmakers. Its intent, as an illustration, is to become the brake-parts supplier that carmakers in India and abroad choose first. Its present plants, skills and customers cannot deliver that yet. The gap is the point: it tells everyone what to build.

Strategic intent is expressed through a hierarchy. Each level supports the one above, so that daily work stays aligned with the long-term vision.

LevelAnswersNature
VisionWhere do we want to be?The future aspiration
MissionWhy do we exist, what do we do and for whom?The organisation's purpose now
GoalsWhat broad results must we achieve?Broad desired outcomes
ObjectivesWhat exactly, by how much and by when?Specific, measurable, time-bound targets

Down the ladder in Pune. A goal is to grow export sales. An objective is, say, to win export orders worth ₹50 crore a year by March 2029. That objective can be handed to a sales head and checked.

Don't confuse strategic intent with a plan. The intent fixes the destination and stays steady for years. The plan says how to get there, and changes as the firm learns. Nor is the intent the same as the vision statement: the vision is one written expression of it.

Where it breaks. A stretch that people see as impossible can demoralise them instead of motivating them. It can also push them to cut corners. And an intent that is never broken down into goals and objectives stays a slogan.

For exams. Know the order of the hierarchy, the question each level answers, and that Hamel and Prahalad (1989) made the term famous.

Go deeper for practitioners

Fit against stretch. Hamel and Prahalad wrote against the idea of strategic fit: trimming ambitions to match the resources a firm already has. They argued that firms which rose to global leadership had started with ambitions far out of proportion to their resources. The gap itself drove them to build new skills and use what they had more cleverly.

A decision. You lead the Pune plant. The board's intent is to be the first-choice brake supplier abroad. Your engineers have never met an export customer's quality audit. Do you bid for a large export order now, or first win a small one to learn the standard? Intent sets the destination; it does not excuse skipping the steps.

Links. The resource-based view (Internal analysis) explains which resources and capabilities a firm can stretch. Levels of strategy (Strategic decisions) show how the intent turns into corporate, business and functional strategy.

Vision, mission, goals, objectives: from aspiration to target.

blocks.title: Vision and mission
blocks.html:
Many offices have two framed statements on the reception wall. Ask the staff how either one changed a decision last month, and most cannot say. Vision and mission are meant to do that work.

In plain wordsA vision says where we want to be one day. A mission says what we do now, for whom, and why.

Exam definitionA standard textbook account: a vision statement describes where the organisation wants to be in future, or should be to best meet its stakeholders' needs. A mission statement describes the role through which it serves its stakeholders: what it does, whom it serves and what makes it distinctive.

The vision describes dreams and aspirations. It gives a shared sense of direction and guides decisions and planning. An effective vision is:

  • clear and unambiguous;
  • in harmony with the organisation's culture and values;
  • realistic;
  • short enough to remember;
  • shared by everyone in the organisation.

The mission states the organisation's present capabilities, whom it serves and what makes it distinctive. It provides the frame within which strategies are made. It is usually written at the top, with the chief executive's lead, though units may have their own. A mission may need redefining as the organisation grows, but its fundamentals should be kept.

Example. Here are two statements for an imagined district dairy cooperative, written as an illustration:

  • Vision: every home in the district drinks fresh, fairly priced milk from its own farmers.
  • Mission: we collect milk twice a day from our member farmers, test and pack it, and deliver it to homes and shops within hours. We pay farmers on time and return the surplus to them. We aim to reach every village in the district.

The mission shows the usual three parts: the purpose (fresh milk from member farmers to local buyers), the core values that shape behaviour (prompt, fair payment), and the main goals (reach every village).

AspectVisionMission
QuestionWhere do we want to be?What do we do, for whom, and why?
TimeThe futureThe present
PurposeInspire and give directionDefine scope and purpose; frame strategy

A good mission is feasible, clear enough to act on, inspiring, precise (neither too broad nor too narrow), distinctive and credible to all stakeholders. "We serve customers" is too broad; "we sell toned milk in 500 ml packets" is too narrow to guide growth.

Don't confuse the mission with the vision. A quick test: if the statement is already true today, it is a mission; if it describes something not yet reached, it is a vision.

Where it breaks. Many statements are so general that they could hang in any firm's office. Others are written once and never used. A statement guides nothing unless goals, budgets and daily choices follow from it.

In practice. Test a mission by using it to turn down an opportunity. If the dairy is offered a contract to supply milk powder abroad, does the mission say yes, no, or nothing? For exams, learn the vision–mission contrast, the three parts of a mission and the qualities of a good one.

Vision looks ahead; mission says what we do now.

blocks.title: Goals and objectives
blocks.html:
A bank branch manager is told to "improve customer service". A year later she says it improved and her regional head says it did not. Neither can prove it, because nobody turned the goal into an objective.

In plain wordsA goal is a broad result we want. An objective is a precise target: what, how much and by when.

Exam definitionA standard textbook account: a goal is a desired future state that the organisation tries to reach. Objectives are the specific targets it aims to reach over a period.

Goals make the mission concrete and coordinate the work of different departments. Well-made goals:

  • are precise and measurable;
  • address critical issues;
  • are realistic yet challenging;
  • are to be reached within a set time;
  • include non-financial as well as financial results.

Objectives are the foundation of planning, and policies are made to achieve them. Top management sets them. Effective objectives are multiple rather than single, and cover both the short and the long term. They are flexible enough to respond to change, and feasible and operational.

The SMART test. A good objective is specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound. The acronym comes from George Doran (1981). He had ‘assignable’, meaning saying who will do it, where ‘achievable’ now usually stands.

Example. The branch's goal is better customer service. One objective, as an illustration: cut the average wait at the cash counter from 20 minutes to 12 minutes by 31 March, measured from token times. That is a cut of 8 minutes, and 8 ÷ 20 = 40%.

TestHow the branch objective meets it
SpecificOne service, the cash counter, and one measure, waiting time
MeasurableToken times show the average wait each day
AchievableOpening a second counter at peak hours can plausibly save 8 minutes
RealisticThe branch has the staff to open that counter
Time-boundBy 31 March

Objectives also differ by horizon.

HorizonTypical areas
Long-termCompetitive position, technological leadership, profitability, return on investment, employee relations and productivity, corporate image
Short-termImmediate steps that support them, such as where to locate a store, its size, the number of staff and the launch marketing plan

Don't confuse goals with objectives. "Improve customer service" is a goal: broad, with no number or date. "Cut the average wait to 12 minutes by 31 March" is an objective. A goal can have several objectives under it.

Where it breaks. A single number invites people to hit the number and miss the point. Staff could cut waiting time by rushing customers and making more errors. That is why objectives should be multiple: pair the waiting-time target with one for errors.

For exams. Expand SMART, know Doran's original ‘assignable’, and tell a goal from an objective in an example.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why specific targets work. Edwin Locke and Gary Latham's goal-setting research found that specific, difficult goals usually lead to higher performance than vague ones such as "do your best". People also need feedback on progress and must accept the goal. Motivation theories (Unit 2) cover this in more depth.

Objectives that pull against each other. Profit and market share, or speed and accuracy, often conflict. Setting both does not settle the conflict. Managers still have to decide which one gives way, and say so in advance.

A decision. By February the branch's average wait is down to 11 minutes, but customer complaints about errors have doubled. Do you report the objective as met? The SMART test is passed; the goal, better service, is not. Report both, and add an error objective for next year.

Goals make the mission concrete; objectives make goals measurable.

text: Strategic intent sets an aspiration beyond present resources. The Kuṟaḷ asks that every thought be of rising high, and says that such aims keep their worth even when they fail. The couplet is about a person's ambition, not an organisation's competitive goal.

text: Good objectives are challenging but feasible. The Kuṟaḷ warns that many who did not know their own strength set out in a rush of zeal and broke down halfway. Read beside the previous couplet, it marks the other limit: aim high, but within what can be done.
pairings.quote: “Many, not knowing their own strength, set out in a rush of zeal and broke down halfway.” உடைத்தம் வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 473

chapters.title: Strategic Decisions and Levels of Strategy
chapters.scope: What makes a decision strategic, and how strategy is made at the corporate, business, functional and operating levels.

blocks.title: What makes a decision strategic
blocks.html:
An auto-parts maker in Pune must decide whether to start making parts for electric vehicles. That choice will tie up crores of rupees for a decade. Choosing next week's shift roster ties up nothing. Only the first is strategic.

In plain wordsA strategic decision is a big, hard-to-reverse choice about where the whole organisation is going.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: strategic decisions are made in line with the organisation's mission and goals; they commit major resources and shape its future direction and scope.

Characteristics. Strategic decisions:

  • commit major resources, whether acquiring new ones or reorganising and reallocating existing ones;
  • match the organisation's capabilities to the threats and opportunities around it;
  • define the scope of its activities: what it wants to be, and to be about;
  • involve major change, are complex, and are made at the top;
  • carry much uncertainty and risk, because they concern the future. Managers must think through scenarios that may or may not happen.

H. Igor Ansoff (Corporate Strategy, 1965) distinguished three kinds of decision.

AspectStrategicAdministrativeOperational
Made byTop managementMiddle managementLower and operating management
Time spanLong termMedium termShort term
FrequencyInfrequent, often one-offPeriodicDaily, routine
Guided byThe mission and visionStrategic decisionsStrategic and administrative decisions
Concerned withThe direction, scope and growth of the whole organisationStructuring and organising resources and people to carry out strategyEfficient day-to-day production and service

Back to the Pune plant. Deciding to make parts for electric vehicles, or to compete on cost, is strategic. Setting up a new division and moving engineers and budget into it is administrative. Scheduling shifts and ordering materials within the new budget is operational.

Don't confuse "strategic" with "expensive". Replacing a worn-out machine can cost lakhs, yet it changes neither direction nor scope, so it is not strategic. Study notes sometimes swap the time spans and frequencies of the last two types. Administrative decisions are medium term and periodic; operational ones are short term and daily.

Where it breaks. The three types are a simplification. In a small firm the owner makes all three. Many small operational choices, repeated, can add up to a direction nobody chose; Henry Mintzberg called strategy that forms this way "emergent".

In practice. Before a big choice, ask: does it change what we do or for whom, does it commit a large share of our resources, and can we undo it cheaply? Two yes answers mean it belongs at the top. For exams, match each type to who makes it, its time span and its frequency.

Strategic decisions are few, far-reaching and hard to reverse.

blocks.title: Four levels of strategy
blocks.html:
A family group runs a cement plant, a hotel chain and a dairy. Whether to sell the hotels, how the dairy should beat local rivals, and how the dairy's plant should cut waste are questions for different people.

In plain wordsLevels of strategy are the layers at which a company plans, from the whole group down to a single plant.

Exam definitionA standard textbook account: in a diversified company, strategy is made at the corporate, business, functional and operational levels, and each level's strategy is formulated in line with the one above it.

A diversified company has several lines of business under one umbrella. Each level of strategy is named after the level that makes it.

LevelQuestion it answersMade by
CorporateWhich industries and markets should we be in, and how should resources be divided among them?Top management and the board
BusinessHow should this business compete in its market?Heads of strategic business units (SBUs)
FunctionalHow will each department (production, marketing, finance, HR) support the business strategy and get the most from its resources?Functional heads
OperationalHow will a plant, sales territory or section meet its immediate targets?Operating and field managers, with help from middle managers

Corporate strategy sets long-term direction and affects every business under the umbrella. Business strategy is formulated in line with it. Functional strategies support the business strategy. Operating strategies carry out the functional ones, often one for each set of annual objectives.

Example. A business that competes on low cost needs a production strategy that cuts operating costs. It needs an HR strategy that keeps a lean workforce of highly qualified people. Its marketing and financial strategies must fit the same aim.

Don't confuse corporate strategy with business strategy. Corporate strategy asks which businesses to be in. Business strategy asks how one of them wins. In a single-business firm the two levels merge.

Where it breaks. The neat cascade suggests strategy only flows down. In practice ideas also flow up: a plant manager's way of cutting cost can reshape how the whole business competes.

For exams. Match a question to its level, and each level to who makes it.

Corporate: where to compete. Business: how to compete. Functional and operational: how to deliver.

blocks.title: Business-level strategy: competing and cooperating
blocks.html:
Three chai stalls share a road. One sells the cheapest cup at ₹10; another sells ₹30 masala chai with fresh snacks; the third tries to be both, and loses customers to each. Business-level strategy is the choice the third stall never made.

In plain wordsBusiness-level strategy is how one business plans to win customers from its rivals.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: business strategy is the set of actions a business unit uses to gain a competitive advantage, the ability to outperform its rivals, in a particular market.

It is made up of competitive strategies, which aim to win customers away from rivals, and cooperative strategies, in which a firm works with others to gain advantage together. Lasting success needs a sustainable competitive advantage, one rivals cannot quickly copy.

Michael Porter (Competitive Strategy, 1980) named three generic strategies, set by two choices: compete on cost or on uniqueness, and target the broad market or a narrow segment. The third strategy, focus, comes in a cost and a differentiation form, which gives four cells.

StrategyTargetSource of advantage
Cost leadershipBroad marketThe lowest costs in the industry, allowing lower prices or higher margins
DifferentiationBroad marketUnique features that customers value and will pay a premium for
Cost focusA narrow segmentLower cost in serving that segment
Differentiation focusA narrow segmentMeeting that segment's special needs better than broad competitors

Porter warned that a firm trying to do everything without committing to one of these risks being stuck in the middle, with no clear advantage. That was the third chai stall.

Blue ocean strategy (W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, 2005) takes another route. Instead of fighting rivals in existing markets, the ‘red oceans’, it creates uncontested market space where competition is irrelevant.

Key success factors are the few things in an industry that most decide whether a firm can compete successfully. Examples are distribution reach in packaged foods and reliability in airlines.

Don't confuse a focus strategy with simply being small. Focus is a deliberate choice of a narrow segment, served on cost or on uniqueness. A small firm that sells a bit of everything to everyone has no focus.

Where it breaks. Later writers questioned "stuck in the middle". Some firms combine low cost and differentiation, for example when better quality also cuts waste and rework. And any advantage wears away as rivals copy it.

For exams. Know the two choices behind the grid, the four cells, and the authors and years of the generic strategies and blue ocean strategy.

Go deeper for practitioners

Neither choice is absolute. Porter also argued that a cost leader cannot ignore quality: its product must stay close enough to rivals' that buyers do not demand a deep discount. A differentiator, in turn, must keep its costs near rivals', or its price premium is eaten by higher costs.

A decision. You run a regional snacks brand. A national rival has wider distribution, which is the key success factor in packaged foods. Matching its reach would cost crores. The alternative is a focus strategy: one region's tastes, served better than a national brand bothers to. Which advantage can you defend for five years?

Links. Porter's five forces (External analysis) explain why some industries leave more room for any strategy. The resource-based view and VRIO (Internal analysis) ask whether an advantage can last.

Low cost or different; broad or focused.

text: In deep water the crocodile overcomes all others; out of the water, others overcome it. A focus strategy rests on the same insight: choose the segment where your strengths decide the contest. The couplet is about choosing a battleground, not a market.
pairings.quote: “In deep water the crocodile prevails; out of the water, others prevail over it.” நெடும்புனலுள் வெல்லும் முதலை அடும்புனலின் நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற. Tirukkuṟaḷ 495

chapters.title: External Analysis: PESTEL, Five Forces and Industry Life Cycle
chapters.scope: How a firm reads the world outside it: the macro-environment, the forces that shape competition in its industry, and the industry's stage of life.

blocks.title: What external analysis is
blocks.html:
When the Covid-19 lockdowns closed dining rooms, a restaurant that already knew the delivery apps could turn itself into a cloud kitchen quickly. One that had watched only its own kitchen started from nothing.

In plain wordsExternal analysis is studying what is happening outside the firm that could help or hurt it.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: external (environmental) analysis examines the industry and the wider macro-environment to identify the opportunities and threats that will drive the firm's profitability, growth and volatility.

It works at two levels:

  • Industry level: the industry's competitive structure, the firm's competitive position, and the industry's dynamics and history.
  • Macro level: economic, global, political, social, demographic and technological conditions.

Example. For a kirana store, the industry level covers the new supermarket nearby and grocery delivery apps. The macro level covers rising incomes, digital payments and changing food habits.

Benefits. It encourages growth into new areas. It helps the firm anticipate and adapt to change, as restaurants that turned to cloud kitchens did. And it shows where the firm can set itself apart from competitors.

ElementWhat to examine
Supply chainThe whole path from raw materials to finished goods reaching the customer, compared with industry benchmarks
IndustryIts present risks and opportunities, current size, projected growth, and alternative industries to explore
Economic trendsInterest rates, inflation, trade rules and the risk of recession, and how they will affect profits
CompetitorsThe forces that set the level of competition (Porter's five forces)
Market demographicsCustomers' age, income, location, interests, and how the product improves their lives
Industry life cycleThe stage the industry has reached
PEST or PESTELThe broad political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal setting

Environmental scanning, the first step of the strategic management process, is the continuing search for this information.

Don't confuse external analysis with internal analysis. External analysis asks how outside factors, such as industry trends, affect the business; it finds opportunities and threats. Internal analysis looks at the business itself, its resources, processes and culture; it finds strengths and weaknesses. Strategy needs both.

Where it breaks. The future is uncertain, and frameworks give a snapshot of a moving scene. Managers also tend to notice the signals they expect and dismiss the rest.

For exams. The purpose is to find opportunities and threats; scanning is the first step of the strategic management process.

blocks.title: PEST and PESTEL analysis
blocks.html:
A two-wheeler maker planning five years ahead must ask more than "will buyers like the model?". Subsidies, loan rates, battery costs and emission rules could each change the answer.

In plain wordsPESTEL is a checklist of six kinds of change in the world around a business.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: PEST analysis examines the political, economic, social and technological factors in a firm's macro-environment; PESTEL extends it with environmental and legal factors.

It is used in corporate planning and to weigh the pros and cons of a business strategy. The last column applies each factor to the two-wheeler maker, as an illustration.

FactorExamplesFor a two-wheeler maker
PoliticalTax policy, trade restrictions, tariffs, bureaucracy, government stabilityA government subsidy for electric scooters is raised or withdrawn
EconomicGrowth rates, interest rates, exchange rates, inflation, unemploymentHigher interest rates make vehicle loans dearer
SocialCulture and perceptions, health consciousness, population growth, age distribution, attitudes to careersMore young people take delivery jobs that need a scooter
TechnologicalR&D activity, automation, technology incentives, the rate of technological changeCheaper, longer-lasting batteries
EnvironmentalWeather, climate change, pollution, natural disasters such as floods, droughts and heat waves, and the growing pressure for sustainable operationsCity air pollution pushes buyers and regulators towards electric models
LegalIndustry regulation, licences and permits, labour laws, consumer protection, competition law, intellectual propertyStricter emission and safety standards for new models

Using it. List the changes under each factor. Then rank them by how likely each is and how much it would hurt or help. The top few become the opportunities and threats in a SWOT.

Don't confuse political with legal factors. Political factors concern the relationship between business and government. Legal factors are the laws that define what a business may or may not do. They meet when government passes legislation that changes how businesses operate.

Where it breaks. PESTEL is a list, not an analysis. It can produce long lists with no priorities. The factors also interact: a pollution problem (environmental) often becomes a new rule (legal).

For exams. Expand the letters, classify examples into factors, and know which two PESTEL adds to PEST. PESTLE is the same six in another order.

Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal.

blocks.title: Porter's five forces
blocks.html:
Airlines carry millions of passengers, yet Porter named airlines as an industry where almost no firm earns attractive returns. The reason lies not only in rivals but in four other forces.

In plain wordsThe five forces are five sources of pressure that decide how much profit an industry leaves for its firms.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: five competitive forces together set an industry's competitive intensity, and so its profit potential. They are the threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of suppliers, the bargaining power of buyers, the threat of substitutes, and rivalry among existing competitors.

Michael Porter set out the model in the Harvard Business Review in 1979. Where the forces are intense, as in airlines, almost no firm earns attractive returns. Where they are mild, as in soft drinks, there is room for higher returns.

ForceStronger (worse for the industry) when…Example
Threat of new entrantsEntry barriers are low. Barriers include economies of scale, brand loyalty, large capital needs, accumulated experience, government licensing and limited access to distribution.Low to medium in airlines and telecom: aircraft, spectrum and licences cost a great deal
Bargaining power of suppliersSuppliers are few or concentrated, inputs have no substitutes, switching suppliers is costly, or the supplier's product is uniqueVery high in airlines, which depend on a few makers of aircraft and on fuel
Bargaining power of buyersBuyers are few or buy in bulk, products are standard, and switching is cheap. Online price comparison has raised buyer power.High in mobile phones and FMCG
Threat of substitutesOther products meet the same need at a better price-performance and switching is easyEnergy drinks and coffee both meet the need to stay alert
Rivalry among existing competitorsCompetitors are many and of similar size, growth is slow, switching costs are low, fixed costs are high, and exit barriers (long-term loans, specialised assets) keep firms in. A low concentration ratio signals intense rivalry.High in Indian aviation: low-cost carriers, high fixed costs and similar-sized players

Reading the concentration ratio. It is the combined market share of the largest few firms. Suppose, as an illustration, the four largest firms hold 20%, 15%, 10% and 5%:

CR4 = 20 + 15 + 10 + 5 = 50%

Half the market is spread among many smaller firms, so no few firms dominate and rivalry is likely to be strong. If the top four held 90%, a few large firms would dominate.

Firms can reduce buyer power through loyalty programmes and differentiation, and entry threat by building scale and brand.

A sixth factor: complementors. Some writers add the power of firms that make complements, products that add value to the industry's own. Andy Grove of Intel proposed it as a sixth force; Adam Brandenburger and Barry Nalebuff's Co-opetition (1996) put complementors in their ‘value net’. Weak or unattractive complements can slow an industry's growth. Porter treats complements as a factor that affects the five forces rather than a force of its own.

Don't confuse substitutes with rivals. A rival sells the same product: another airline on the same route. A substitute meets the same need in a different way: a train, a bus, or a video call instead of the trip.

Where it breaks. The model is a snapshot, and industry boundaries are often unclear. It treats other firms mainly as threats, which is why complementors were added. It also explains industry profit, not why one firm in the industry beats another.

For exams. Name the five forces, say what makes each stronger, and know the debate over complementors as a sixth force.

Go deeper for practitioners

Factors, not forces. In a 2008 Harvard Business Review article Porter listed four things often mistaken for forces: the industry's growth rate, technology and innovation, government, and complementary products. Each matters only through its effect on the five forces. A fast-growing industry, for example, is not attractive if suppliers are powerful and entry is easy.

A decision. You are asked to open cafés in a growing city. Growth looks good, but check the forces: rents are set by a few landlords (supplier power), customers can switch at no cost (buyer power), entry is cheap, and tea stalls are a substitute. Unless a brand or location raises a barrier, growth alone will not bring profit.

Links. The industry life cycle (next) shows how the forces change as an industry ages. Integration strategies (Corporate strategies) are one way to reduce supplier or buyer power.

Entrants, suppliers, buyers, substitutes, rivalry.

blocks.title: The industry life cycle
blocks.html:
Price cuts that win customers while a market is growing fast can start a ruinous price war once growth stops. The right move depends on how old the industry is.

In plain wordsIndustries are born, grow, mature and decline, and the rules of competition change at each stage.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the industry life cycle describes the stages an industry passes through over time, from introduction through growth and maturity to decline.

The simple version has four stages: introduction (low sales, high costs), growth (rising sales and profits, new entrants), maturity (saturation) and decline (falling demand, firms leave). Profitability usually peaks in growth and maturity.

Charles Hill and Gareth Jones describe five stages and what each means for competition.

StageCompetitive conditions
Embryonic (start-up)Little competition. Barriers to entry rest on access to key technological know-how rather than scale or brand.
GrowthDemand grows fast. Few firms have scale or brand loyalty yet, so the threat of new entrants is at its highest; but rapid growth absorbs newcomers, so rivalry stays low.
ShakeoutGrowth slows. Rivalry becomes intense, firms cut prices, and weaker ones leave.
MaturityThe market is saturated. Entry barriers rise, so the threat of new entrants falls; firms segment the market and avoid price wars.
DeclineDemand falls. Rivalry among the established firms intensifies, especially where exit barriers are high.

Example. Picture a new kind of product whose sales are climbing fast. Many start-ups enter, yet all of them grow, because demand is rising. When growth slows, the same firms fight over a market that has stopped expanding. That is the shakeout.

Don't say the threat of entry is low in the growth stage. It is a common mistake. In Hill and Jones's account it is at its highest then, though fast growth keeps rivalry low. Also, don't confuse the industry life cycle with the product life cycle: one describes a whole industry, the other a single product.

Where it breaks. Stages vary in length, and the turning points are clear only afterwards. Some industries never follow the curve, because new technology renews demand. Firms' own moves can also speed up or delay a stage.

In practice. In growth, invest to build scale and brand before the shakeout. In maturity, segment and protect margins. In decline, choose between leading the remaining market and leaving early. For exams, learn the five stages and the entry threat and rivalry in each.

Embryonic, growth, shakeout, maturity, decline.

text: The Kuṟaḷ makes it the ruler's work to know quickly everything that happens, to everyone, at all times, and the couplets around it describe the agents who gather that knowledge. Environmental scanning is the same continuing watch over the world outside the organisation.

The Kuṟaḷ likewise asks for four strengths to be weighed before acting: of the task itself, of oneself, of the opponent, and of the allies on each side. chapters.title: Internal Analysis: Resources, Capabilities and SWOT
chapters.scope: How a firm looks inward: the tools of internal analysis, the resource-based view, VRIO, the McKinsey 7-S model, and SWOT and TOWS.

blocks.title: What internal analysis is
blocks.html:
An auto-parts maker in Pune has lost two large orders in a year. Before blaming the market, its managers need to find what is slipping inside the firm: cost, quality, delivery or people.

In plain wordsInternal analysis is a firm's honest look at itself: what it has, what it does well, and what holds it back.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: internal analysis examines the organisation's own resources, assets and processes, tangible and intangible, to find where it can grow or must change.

Paired with external analysis, it shows how the firm works on its own and within its industry. It looks for:

  • strengths: the quality of its people, the resources it has, brand recognition;
  • weaknesses, often structural: poor training, outdated technology, weak communication between departments;
  • opportunities for growth, and likely threats. Threats usually come from outside; the internal view asks how well placed the firm is to meet them;
  • viability: a niche that sets it apart from competitors, often the long-term aim.
ToolWhat it does
Gap analysisFinds the gap between a business goal and the current state; used to locate weaknesses
Strategy evaluationChecks at regular intervals whether the firm is meeting the objectives in its plan
SWOT analysisA broad overview of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
VRIO analysisTests which resources can give a lasting advantage
OCAT (Organisational Capacity Assessment Tool)Rates internal performance on specific dimensions to find areas of strength or growth
McKinsey 7-S frameworkChecks that seven elements of the organisation are aligned
Core competencies analysisIdentifies the combination of abilities that sets the business apart from competitors
Value chain analysisBreaks the firm into activities to find where it creates value and cost

Gap analysis, worked. As an illustration, the Pune plant promises its carmaker customers that 98 of every 100 deliveries will arrive on time. Last quarter only 90 did. The gap is 98 − 90 = 8 percentage points. That is the symptom; the value chain helps find the cause.

The value chain (Michael Porter, Competitive Advantage, 1985) divides a firm's activities into primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service) and support activities (firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development and procurement). Advantage comes from performing these activities at lower cost, or in a way that creates more value than rivals do. Margin is the difference between what customers pay and what all the activities cost.

Back to the Pune plant. Steel arriving late from suppliers is inbound logistics. Machining is operations, and trucks to the carmakers are outbound logistics. If the delays trace back to a production plan nobody updates, the weakness sits in firm infrastructure, a support activity, not on the shop floor.

Don't confuse internal analysis with external analysis. External analysis (PESTEL, the five forces) studies the environment and the industry, which the firm cannot control. Internal analysis studies what the firm can control. Nor is the value chain the supply chain: the value chain is the activities inside one firm; the supply chain links many firms from raw material to customer.

Where it breaks. Firms rate themselves generously, yet a strength counts only if it beats rivals', so comparison with competitors is essential. The value chain was drawn for manufacturers and fits a bank or an online platform less neatly.

In practice. Use a gap analysis to find the symptom, the value chain to find its source, and VRIO to decide which strengths to build on. For exams, learn the five primary and four support activities.

blocks.title: The resource-based view
blocks.html:
Two kirana stores on one street pay the same rent and buy from the same wholesaler. A supermarket opens nearby, and one store keeps its customers while the other loses them. The difference lies in what each has built inside.

In plain wordsA firm wins over the long run because of what it has and knows how to do, not only because of the industry it is in.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the resource-based view holds that sustained competitive advantage comes mainly from the valuable, rare and hard-to-imitate resources and capabilities inside the firm, rather than from its position in the industry.

The resource-based view (RBV) took shape in the 1980s and 1990s in the work of Birger Wernerfelt (“A Resource-Based View of the Firm”, 1984), C. K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel, J.-C. Spender, Robert Grant and Jay Barney.

TypeExamplesAs a source of advantage
TangibleProperty, land, plant, products, financial capitalCan usually be bought on the market, so rivals can match them quickly; they give little lasting advantage
IntangibleReputation and goodwill, brands and trademarks, intellectual property, culture, know-howBuilt over time and not for sale, so hard to imitate; the main source of lasting advantage

Back to the kirana stores. The shelves, the stock and the billing machine are tangible; the supermarket can buy better ones. The store that survives has intangibles the supermarket cannot buy: an owner who knows what each family orders, credit given on trust, and delivery to the door within the hour.

Two assumptions. Resources are heterogeneous: they differ from firm to firm, which is why firms facing the same environment can follow different strategies. And they are immobile: they do not move easily between firms, at least in the short run, so rivals cannot quickly copy them. Intangible resources are more immobile than tangible ones.

Core competence (Prahalad and Hamel, 1990) is a bundle of skills and technologies that lets a firm deliver distinctive value across several businesses. Their three tests: it gives access to a wide variety of markets, it contributes significantly to the benefits customers perceive, and it is difficult for competitors to imitate. Their own example was Honda, whose skill with engines serves its cars, motorcycles, lawn mowers and generators.

Don't confuse the RBV with the positioning view. Porter's five forces work outside-in: pick an attractive industry and a defensible position in it. The RBV works inside-out: build on what the firm has that rivals lack. Nor is a resource the same as a capability. A resource is something the firm has; a capability is what it can do by combining resources.

Where it breaks. Critics, notably Richard Priem and John Butler (2001), argued that the view comes close to a circle: valuable resources give advantage, and resources are called valuable because they give advantage. It says little about how to build such resources, and a resource valuable today can lose its value when markets change.

For exams. Match the names: Wernerfelt (1984) named the view; Prahalad and Hamel (1990) gave core competence; Barney (1991) gave the tests that became VRIO.

Go deeper for practitioners

Dynamic capabilities. David Teece, Gary Pisano and Amy Shuen (1997) answered the charge that the RBV is static. They argued that in fast-changing markets what matters most is a firm's ability to build, combine and reshape its resources, not the stock it holds today.

A decision. The surviving kirana owner has ₹5 lakh to spend. A new air-conditioned shopfront is tangible and the supermarket already has a better one. A phone-ordering service for regular customers builds on the knowledge and trust he already has. The RBV points to the second.

Look inside: lasting advantage lies in what rivals cannot buy or copy.

blocks.title: The VRIO framework
blocks.html:
An auto-parts maker owns a testing rig worth ₹5 crore and calls it a strength. If three of its four rivals own one too, it only keeps the firm level with them. VRIO sorts real advantages from expensive equipment.

In plain wordsVRIO is a four-question test of whether a resource can give a firm a lasting edge.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the VRIO framework (Jay Barney) holds that a resource gives sustained competitive advantage only if it is valuable, rare and costly to imitate, and the firm is organised to exploit it.

Owning heterogeneous, immobile resources is not enough to sustain an advantage. Jay Barney (1991) proposed four tests, VRIN: valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable. Barney later recast them as VRIO, replacing non-substitutability with organisation.

QuestionMeaning
Valuable?Does the resource let the firm raise the value it offers customers, through differentiation or lower cost, or exploit an opportunity or neutralise a threat?
Rare?Is it held by only one or a very few firms? If many have it, it brings only parity.
Costly to imitate?Would rivals find it difficult or expensive to copy or substitute? If not, any advantage is temporary.
Organised to capture value?Are the firm's structure, systems and processes set up to use it fully, for example by putting talented people in the right roles?

Ask the questions in order. Each one matters only if the resource passed the one before, so the first "no" gives the result.

ValuableRareCostly to imitateOrganisedResult
No–––Competitive disadvantage
YesNo––Competitive parity
YesYesNo–Temporary competitive advantage
YesYesYesNoUnused competitive advantage
YesYesYesYesSustained competitive advantage

Two resources of the Pune plant, tested.

  • The testing rig. Valuable: yes, it cuts testing time. Rare: no, most rivals own one. Result: parity. It is needed to stay in the game, not to win.
  • Its engineers' long working ties with carmakers' design teams. Valuable: yes, the firm hears of new models early. Rare: yes. Costly to imitate: yes, such trust takes years to build. Organised: no, because the engineers sit in a back office and are never asked to join bids. Result: unused advantage. The fix is to put them on bid teams.

Using it: identify the firm's potential key resources; test each against the four questions; then develop and nurture those that pass.

Don't confuse VRIO with VRIN. Both start valuable, rare, inimitable. VRIN's fourth test asks whether a substitute exists; VRIO folds substitutes into "costly to imitate" and adds organisation, whether the firm can actually use what it has.

Where it breaks. Each answer is a judgement, and managers tend to rate their own resources highly. The test is a snapshot: a sustained advantage lasts only until technology or customers change. It tells a firm which resources matter, not how to build new ones.

For exams. Expect the result table as a match-the-pairs question. Remember the order and the five outcomes, and that the O was added later in place of the N.

Valuable, Rare, costly to Imitate, Organised.

blocks.title: The McKinsey 7-S framework
blocks.html:
A public-sector bank decides to lend more to small businesses. Its branch staff are still rewarded only for collecting deposits, and few have been trained to judge a loan. A year later the new strategy has hardly moved.

In plain wordsSeven parts of an organisation must fit together; change one and the others usually have to change too.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the McKinsey 7-S framework holds that organisational effectiveness depends on aligning seven interdependent elements: strategy, structure, systems, shared values, style, staff and skills.

The framework comes from Robert Waterman, Tom Peters and Julien Phillips (1980), developed with Richard Pascale and Anthony Athos. It put the ‘soft’ human side of organisations alongside the traditional tangibles of capital and equipment as a key to performance.

ElementTypeMeaning
StrategyHardThe plan for gaining advantage
StructureHardHow the organisation is divided and who reports to whom
SystemsHardThe procedures and processes of daily work
Shared valuesSoftThe core beliefs at the centre, linking all the others
StyleSoftHow leaders behave
StaffSoftThe people and how they are developed
SkillsSoftThe organisation's distinctive capabilities

The hard elements are tangible and easier to define and manage; the soft ones are intangible, shaped by culture, and harder to change. Shared values sit at the centre as the glue. Because the elements are interdependent, a change in one usually needs changes in the others, and misalignment causes friction.

Back to the bank. The strategy changed, but nothing else did:

  • Systems: targets and incentives still count only deposits;
  • Skills and staff: few officers can appraise a small firm's accounts, and none have been trained;
  • Style: branch managers, fearing bad loans, refer every application upward;
  • Shared values: "never let a loan go bad" outweighs "help local businesses grow".

Aligning them means new targets, credit training, a clear limit each branch may approve, and leaders who accept some risk.

Don't confuse the 7 S's with the 7 Ps. The 7 Ps (product, price, place, promotion, people, process, physical evidence) are the marketing mix for services. The 7 S's describe a whole organisation. Within the 7 S's, staff is the people; skills is what the organisation as a whole can do.

Where it breaks. The model says what must fit, not how to change it or in what order. It is a still picture of the inside and says little about customers or competitors.

For exams. Sort the seven into hard and soft, and remember shared values at the centre. Strategy implementation (later in this unit) applies the model to putting a strategy into action.

Hard: strategy, structure, systems. Soft: shared values, style, staff, skills.

blocks.title: SWOT and TOWS
blocks.html:
A chain of 12 chai cafés in Pune hears that a national café chain is coming to town. The owners write down what they have and what they fear. A list alone does not tell them what to do.

In plain wordsSWOT lists what helps and what hurts a firm, inside and outside. TOWS pairs those items to produce strategy options.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: SWOT analysis sums up the internal audit (strengths and weaknesses) and the external audit (opportunities and threats), bridging analysis and strategy formulation.

SourceHelpfulHarmful
InternalStrengths: capabilities and resources that give an advantageWeaknesses: limitations that reduce performance and need improving
ExternalOpportunities: favourable conditions to exploitThreats: unfavourable forces to guard against

The chai chain's SWOT. Strengths: a recipe regulars love and low rents near colleges. Weakness: no online ordering. Opportunities: more people order food through delivery apps, and new office parks are opening. Threat: the national chain.

The TOWS matrix (Heinz Weihrich, 1982) goes one step further: it pairs the internal and external factors to generate strategies.

Internal factorsOpportunitiesThreats
StrengthsSO (maxi-maxi): use strengths to seize opportunitiesST (maxi-mini): use strengths to counter threats
WeaknessesWO (mini-maxi): use opportunities to overcome weaknessesWT (mini-mini): reduce weaknesses and avoid threats
CellOption for the chai chain
SOOpen outlets near the new office parks, leading with the popular recipe
STReward loyal college regulars so they stay when the national chain arrives
WOJoin the delivery apps to make up for having no online ordering
WTClose weak outlets and avoid a price war it cannot afford

Don't confuse a strength with an opportunity. Strengths and weaknesses are inside the firm and under its control. Opportunities and threats are outside. Growing use of delivery apps is an opportunity for the chai chain, not a strength; being on those apps would be a strength.

Where it breaks. A SWOT gives no weights, so a minor point sits beside a decisive one. One fact can land in two boxes: a family-run board may be a strength (quick decisions) and a weakness (few outside views). In a 1997 study, Terry Hill and Roy Westbrook found that the SWOT lists firms drew up were often long and general, and rarely used later.

In practice. Keep each box short, back each item with evidence, and judge strengths against rivals. Then use TOWS to turn the list into options, and evaluate those before choosing.

For exams. Know which factors are internal and which external, the four TOWS cells with their maxi–mini names, and Weihrich (1982).

Go deeper for practitioners

Where the inputs come from. A good SWOT is the last step, not the first. Opportunities and threats come from external analysis (PESTEL, the five forces, the industry life cycle). Strengths and weaknesses come from the value chain, VRIO and comparison with rivals. A SWOT written without that work tends to list opinions.

A decision. The chai chain cannot fund all four options at once. The threat is near and the delivery weakness is cheap to fix, so WO and ST come first. SO needs new outlets and capital, so it waits until the chain knows how its regulars respond to the new rival.

SWOT lists the factors; TOWS turns them into strategies.

text: Book 8 of the Arthaśāstra examines the calamities (vyasana) that can befall each constituent of the state (ruler, ministers, countryside, fort, treasury, army and ally) and debates which is the more serious, so that the ruler knows where to act first. That is an internal audit of weaknesses, ranked by how much harm each does.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 8.1

text: The RBV says advantage comes from knowing and building on what the firm itself has. The Kuṟaḷ says nothing is beyond those who know what they are able to do, learn what must be known, and stay with it. The couplet speaks of a person's capacities; the RBV adds the tests of rarity and imitability.
pairings.quote: “Nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do, learn what is to be known, and hold to it.” ஒல்வ தறிவது அறிந்ததன் கண்தங்கிச் செல்வார்க்குச் செல்லாதது இல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 472

text: Book 9 of the Arthaśāstra opens with knowing the relative strength and weakness of oneself and the enemy in power, place and time before setting out on a campaign. SWOT sets the same comparison, of one's own strengths and weaknesses against the conditions outside, before choosing a course.

chapters.title: Business Portfolio Analysis: BCG and GE–McKinsey Matrices
chapters.scope: How a firm with many businesses decides which to build, hold, harvest or sell.

blocks.title: Designing the business portfolio
blocks.html:
A consumer goods company sells packaged tea, snacks, ready-to-eat meals and agarbattis. It has ₹100 crore to invest this year. Giving each business ₹25 crore looks fair, but it is rarely wise.

In plain wordsA business portfolio is the set of businesses a company owns. Portfolio analysis decides which of them deserve more money, which less and which none.

Exam definitionThe business portfolio is the collection of businesses and products that make up the company. Portfolio analysis is the process by which management evaluates the products and businesses that make up the company (Kotler and Armstrong).

Guided by its mission and objectives, management should plan the portfolio that best fits the company's strengths and weaknesses to the opportunities in its environment. Large firms such as Nestlé or Hindustan Unilever manage complex portfolios of businesses and brands.

Two steps.

  1. Analyse the current portfolio and decide which businesses should get more, less or no investment.
  2. Shape the future portfolio with strategies for growth and for downsizing.

The units analysed are strategic business units (SBUs): a company division, a product line within a division, or sometimes a single product or brand. Each has its own mission and objectives and can be planned independently. In this company, each of the four product lines is an SBU.

Portfolio analysis rates each SBU on two dimensions: the attractiveness of its market or industry, and the strength of its position there. Strong resources go to the more profitable businesses; weaker ones are phased down or dropped. Businesses that fit the firm's core philosophy and competencies deserve support.

SBU (illustration)Market attractivenessIts strength thereFirst view
Packaged teaLow: a mature, slow-growing marketHigh: the market leaderKeep, and use its cash
SnacksHigh: growing fastHigh: a close leaderInvest to keep the lead
Ready-to-eat mealsHigh: growing fastLow: a small playerInvest heavily, or leave
AgarbattisLow: slow growthLow: a small playerRun for cash, or sell

The BCG and GE–McKinsey matrices that follow turn these two ratings into a grid.

Don't confuse an SBU with a department. An SBU faces its own customers and competitors and can be planned on its own. A department, such as finance or HR, serves the whole firm and has no market of its own.

Where it breaks. Portfolio analysis treats each business as separate, yet many share plants, brands, buyers and sales teams. Selling one can raise the others' costs. Formal analysis also takes time and money, and it classifies today's businesses better than it plans tomorrow's.

In practice. Use the ratings to start the argument about where money goes, not to end it. Ask what each business shares with the others before cutting it.

Rate each business on market attractiveness and its own strength.

blocks.title: The BCG growth-share matrix
blocks.html:
The consumer goods company's tea business earns more cash than it can usefully reinvest. Its ready-meals business burns cash and may never lead its market. The BCG matrix shows how one can pay for the other.

In plain wordsThe BCG matrix sorts a company's businesses by how fast their markets grow and how big they are against the largest rival.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the BCG growth-share matrix classifies strategic business units by market growth rate and relative market share into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.

The Boston Consulting Group developed it under Bruce Henderson around 1970. Each SBU is placed by its market growth rate (the vertical axis, a measure of market attractiveness) and its relative market share (the horizontal axis, a measure of strength). Each SBU is drawn as a circle whose area is proportional to its sales.

Relative market share = the SBU's market share ÷ the share of its largest competitor

For the market leader, the comparison is with the next-largest firm. A common textbook convention draws the dividing lines at 10% market growth and a relative share of 1.0.

CellGrowth and shareCashUsual strategy
StarHigh growth, high shareEarns much but needs heavy investment to keep up with growthBuild or hold
Cash cowLow growth, high shareEstablished; needs little investment and produces surplus cash to fund other SBUsHold, or harvest (‘milk’)
Question mark (problem child)High growth, low shareNeeds a lot of cash just to hold its shareBuild into a star, or phase out
DogLow growth, low shareMay generate enough cash to maintain itself, but no moreHarvest or divest

The company's SBUs, worked. The figures are illustrative.

SBUMarket growthOwn share ÷ rival's shareRelative shareCell
Packaged tea3%30% ÷ 15% (next largest)2.0Cash cow
Snacks15%25% ÷ 20% (next largest)1.25Star
Ready-to-eat meals20%5% ÷ 25% (leader)0.2Question mark
Agarbattis2%4% ÷ 20% (leader)0.2Dog

For each SBU the firm can build share by investing more, hold share at its current level, harvest short-term cash flow whatever the long-term effect, or divest by selling or phasing it out and using the resources elsewhere.

Movement over time. Many SBUs start as question marks, become stars if they succeed, turn into cash cows as market growth slows, and finally become dogs. The firm needs a steady flow of new products so that some become stars and later cash cows that fund the rest.

Don't confuse relative market share with market share. A 20% share makes a firm a leader if the next rival has 10% (relative share 2.0). The same 20% makes it a follower if the leader has 40% (relative share 0.5).

Where it breaks. Two single measures stand in for attractiveness and strength. High market share does not always mean high profit. A ‘dog’ may still have strategic value, for example if it completes a range that shops want to stock whole. The result also depends on how the market is defined: draw it narrowly enough and almost any brand leads.

For exams. Expect a description to place in a cell, the four strategies, and the usual path from question mark to dog. Check which way the share axis runs before answering.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why share mattered to BCG. The matrix rests on BCG's experience curve: unit costs tend to fall by a steady percentage each time a firm's cumulative output (all it has ever produced) doubles. The leader has usually produced the most, so it should have the lowest costs and the most cash. Where costs do not fall much with volume, high share is a weaker sign of strength.

A decision. The company can fund one fast-growing business properly, not two. Ready-to-eat meals sits in a market growing at 20%, but the leader is five times its size. If the company cannot see a way to close in on the leader, BCG's logic says phase it out and put the money into snacks, the star.

Stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs: build, hold, harvest, divest.

blocks.title: The GE–McKinsey nine-cell matrix
blocks.html:
The snacks market grows at 15% a year, so the BCG matrix calls it attractive. But it is crowded, margins are thin and big retailers set the terms. Growth alone overstates how attractive it is.

In plain wordsThe GE–McKinsey matrix rates each business on many factors, not one, and places it in one of nine boxes.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the GE–McKinsey matrix plots each SBU by industry attractiveness and business unit strength, each a weighted score of several factors, on a nine-cell grid that indicates whether to invest, hold or harvest.

McKinsey and Company developed it in the early 1970s for General Electric, which needed a way to decide where to invest across its many SBUs. It plots industry (market) attractiveness on the vertical axis against business unit strength (competitive position) on the horizontal axis.

Each axis is a weighted score built from several factors, then divided into high, medium and low. That gives a 3 × 3 grid of nine cells, a finer assessment than the BCG's four.

AxisTypical factors
Industry attractiveness (external)Market size and growth rate, profitability, pricing trends, competitive intensity, buyer and supplier power, entry barriers and the threat of substitutes, overall risk, demand variability, room to differentiate, technology development
Business unit strength (internal)Market share and its growth, profit margins, cash flow and relative cost position, brand strength and customer loyalty, quality and innovation, financial resources, management strength

A weighted score, worked. The company scores its snacks business. Weights add up to 1; ratings run from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). All figures are illustrative.

FactorWeightRatingWeight × rating
Industry attractiveness

Profitability0.330.9
Competitive intensity (5 = mild)0.320.6
Total1.03.1

Market share0.542.0
